transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-06-05
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood BD); Miguel Torres (LyraGrid Head of Partnerships), Sofia Chen (LyraGrid Cloud Product Lead), Evan Brooks (Sales Director), Anita Rao (Solutions Architect)

Summary (auto): Intro + high level capabilities, partner motions (resell, co-sell, referral), initial technical compatibility notes around NVLinks, PCIe, driver/OS images and inference runtime. Agreed to technical deep-dive and initial benchmark exchange.

Topics:
- Partner program model (resell vs managed offering)
- Hardware stack and GPU SKUs (A100/H100 equivalence, custom blades)
- Network topology options (VPC peering, private link, on-prem colos)
- Security and compliance (SOC2, audit logs, KMS)
- Pilot/benchmark plan and timelines

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on the partner team, with me is Priya our SE and Jordan from partnerships. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Miguel Torres: Good, good. Thanks for setting this up, Miguel from LyraGrid. We're excited to explore how we could partner on end-to-end GPU infra for inference.
[00:13] Sofia Chen: Hi all, Sofia here, Cloud product -- I'll be the product lead coordinating the integration side.
[00:18] Priya Patel: Great, thanks. Quick agenda, we'll cover partner motions, high level technical fit, and then dig into infra compatibility and a pilot blueprint. Open to adjust.
[00:27] Evan Brooks: Sounds good. I'm Evan on Partnerships / Sales. We want to get a sense of level of effort and time to revenue.
[00:33] Alex Kim: Perfect. To kick off — LyraGrid can you give a quick overview of your infra + go-to-market? I know you're a GPU vendor and also run managed clusters?
[00:42] Miguel Torres: Yeah, short answer: we build modular GPU blades, mix of H100-equivalent and Ampere-class blades, sold direct to cloud operators and also as managed clusters in three regions: us-west, eu-central, ap-southeast. We have a partner channel for resellers, and are pushing into OEM for telco.
[00:55] Alex Kim: Nice. When you say managed clusters, is that fully managed (you handle OS/drivers/kubernetes) or do customers run their own control plane?
[01:05] Miguel Torres: We offer both. For smaller customers we do full managed with our control plane. For bigger enterprise customers, we integrate into customer K8s and provide a node pool + operator. There's some variance in how we expose images and drivers.
[01:18] Priya Patel: Ok that matters for how Redwood Dedicated or Private would slot in. We usually run a runtime on top of the infra that depends on consistent CUDA drivers, NCCL for multi-GPU, and support for certain kernel versions for quantized runtimes. Do you standardize an image?
[01:32] Anita Rao: We have a base image but clients occasionally want custom images; we can provide an image catalog and also support bringing-your-own-image. There's some drift we see though between managed and BYO.
[01:43] [slight crosstalk]
[01:47] Priya Patel: That's pretty typical. For us, the biggest friction is NVLink topology and driver parity — if NVLink between GPUs is variable, some model sharding and kv cache strategies change. Does LyraGrid expose NVLink topologies?
[01:59] Miguel Torres: Yes, on our blades we expose NVLink in the same-rack pairs; cross-rack NVLink isn't available yet but we have high bandwidth fabric.
[02:08] Sofia Chen: One question from our infra team — Redwood mentions Dedicated vs Private. What exactly is the differentiation operationally?
[02:16] Alex Kim: Sure, short answer: Redwood Dedicated is reserved capacity in our managed pools with customer isolation and committed throughput; Private is a deployment option where the Redwood control plane can be placed in the customer's VPC or on-prem — customer owns the infra network, we provide the platform binaries and ops guidance. For some partners you'd run Redwood Private on top of your cluster if you want to resell a managed Redwood-powered product.
[02:36] Evan Brooks: So if LyraGrid wants to resell Redwood + infra as a joint offering, would that be a resell or referral?
[02:43] Jordan Li: We have both tracks. Resell is tighter commercial coupling — LyraGrid would bill and manage the customer and we'd support. Referral is lighter weight. We can share the standard partner agreement and margins.
[02:52] Miguel Torres: That makes sense. From a tech standpoint, we want to understand compatibility and whether Redwood requires changes to our images.
[02:58] Priya Patel: In general Redwood's runtime is fairly portable but we do recommend specific CUDA + cuDNN versions and tuned kernels for quantized paths. We also use some custom kernels for attention ops when running int8/4. Sharing kernel-compatibility docs early helps.
[03:14] Sofia Chen: Do you have any hard requirements on orchestration? Like do you require a specific k8s operator or can we expose through an API?
[03:22] Priya Patel: We can run on standard Kubernetes; we usually deploy a small agent/operator for lifecycle and version pinning of the model runtime, but we can also run in a containerized mode behind an API gateway for managed customers.
[03:31] [00:03:31] Miguel Torres: How does billing work for Dedicated? Is it per-GPU-hour? Token based?
[03:37] Alex Kim: Good question — hosted API is per-token, Dedicated is usually capacity or vCPU/GPU reserved billing (monthly commits). For a partner-resell deal we can present blended pricing options.
[03:45] Evan Brooks: And what about latency SLOs? Many of our customers are latency-sensitive for chatbots.
[03:50] Priya Patel: Redwood Optimize and our runtime support latency SLOs. For close-to-infra, we can hit p99 latencies sub-100ms for smaller models and a few hundred ms for large LLMs depending on sequence length and batching. But key is co-location and network (and of course model size/quantization).
[04:06] Sofia Chen: Are there examples of partners who've run Redwood Private on their colos?
[04:10] Alex Kim: Yes, we've run Private in a few telco and finance customers with partners who provide colo or on-prem racks. We have an onboarding checklist for drivers, kernel versions, KMS integration, and audit log forwarding.
[04:21] Miguel Torres: Security — we need to know what certifications Redwood has, can you support SOC2 and provide audit logs + KMS?
[04:28] Alex Kim: We have SOC2, and in Private mode we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll share our security datasheet.
[04:35] [short pause]
[04:38] Priya Patel: One practical thing — for an initial compatibility test we'd like: access to a single LyraGrid node or image, ability to run a quick micro-benchmark (latency + throughput), and sample traces for nvlink topology and dmesg/driver versions. That tells us if kernel-level tuning is needed.
[04:54] Anita Rao: We can stand that up. We usually can provide a test node or a container image in under a week for partners.
[05:01] Alex Kim: Great. We'll send a benchmark template — Priya will own that.
[05:04] Miguel Torres: On go-to-market, we'd like to discuss co-marketing and joint customer pilots. Do you have an enablement kit for partners?
[05:12] Jordan Li: Yes, we have a partner portal, partner playbooks, and co-marketing funds for strategic pilots. We'll share a partner one-pager and recommended pricing tiers.
[05:20] Evan Brooks: Quick nit — any restrictions on model catalog? Some large customers care whether we run closed-source models or a specific LLM.
[05:28] Alex Kim: We support both open models and customer-provided models; listing in the model catalog is curated but we can onboard custom models in Private deployments. For hosted we have some restrictions around IP and content policies.
[05:40] Sofia Chen: Network connectivity: can Redwood support VPC peering and PrivateLink? Some of our enterprise prospects require private network connectivity.
[05:46] Priya Patel: Yes, Private supports VPC peering, PrivateLink, and direct connect variants — we can document recommended network configs.
[05:54] Miguel Torres: Regarding hardware — are there strong benefits to H100-like NVLink vs just faster PCIe for inference workloads? Some customers we talk to care about multi-GPU sharding.
[06:02] Priya Patel: For very large models and sharded KV cache, NVLink topology matters a lot. For single-GPU or model-parallelism that doesn't rely on cross-GPU comms, PCIe can be fine. We'll tailor recommendations per workload.
[06:15] [small chuckle]
[06:17] Alex Kim: Ok, sounds like immediate next steps are: share partner deck, benchmark template, and arrange tech deep-dive with LyraGrid infra. Anything else?
[06:25] Miguel Torres: Can you also include a sample SOW for a pilot and a price schedule? That helps our biz folks evaluate quickly.
[06:32] Alex Kim: Yep. We'll include a sample SOW and a couple of example commercial models (referral/resell).
[06:37] Sofia Chen: Timeline — assuming we run a short benchmark and a 4-week pilot, we could be in a joint pilot by late June if both teams align.
[06:45] Alex Kim: Sounds realistic. We'll put a proposed date in the follow-up.
[06:48] Priya Patel: Anything else from the tech side?
[06:50] Anita Rao: One ask — do you have any reference architectures for running Redwood on edge colos? That's relevant to a telco use-case.
[06:58] Priya Patel: We do; I'll include an edge reference arch and notes about footprint per model.
[07:05] Evan Brooks: Ok cool. Appreciate the time.
[07:08] Alex Kim: Thanks everyone — we'll send notes and docs shortly.
[07:11] [meeting wraps]
